Witch
WICH
noun
From the Old English wicce (feminine) and wicca (masculine), a practitioner of sorcery. The very name of modern “Wicca” is that old word revived; but Scripture knows no harmless witch and no good one.

Biblical Definition

A witch is a practitioner of sorcery — one who works evil, divines, or curses by pact with unclean spirits. The Old English wicce lies behind our word, and the name of modern “Wicca” is that old term revived; but Scripture knows no harmless witch and no good one. The law is stark and unrepeated in its severity: “Thou shalt not suffer a witch to live” (Exo 22:18) — a sentence that measures how deadly God counts the sin, a treason against His sole right to be sought and obeyed. She stands in the forbidden roll beside the enchanter and the wizard: there shall not be found among you “an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch” (Deu 18:10). So grave is the offence that Samuel makes it the very yardstick of rebellion against God’s word: “rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry” (1Sa 15:23) — to defy the LORD is, in its kind, to practise sorcery. And Nahum names doomed Nineveh “the mistress of witchcrafts, that selleth nations through her whoredoms” (Nah 3:4) — witchcraft enslaves whole peoples, and God razes the city that trades in it. The witch is not a fairy-tale but a rebel against heaven; and the only deliverance from her craft is the blood of Christ, who spoiled the very powers she serves.

Webster 1828 Definition

A woman (or man) who practices sorcery by compact with evil spirits — a worker of witchcraft, never benign.

WITCH, a person who practices sorcery or enchantment by supposed compact with evil spirits.

From Old English wicce (feminine) and wicca (masculine), a worker of sorcery.

The law commands that a witch shall not be suffered to live (Exo 22:18).

Samuel makes witchcraft the measure of all rebellion against the word of the LORD (1Sa 15:23).

Nahum calls Nineveh the mistress of witchcrafts that sells nations (Nah 3:4).

Key Scripture

Exo 22:18 — "Thou shalt not suffer a witch to live."

Deu 18:10 — "There shall not be found among you any one that maketh his son or his daughter to pass through the fire, or that useth divination, or an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch,"

1Sa 15:23 — "For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry. Because thou hast rejected the word of the LORD, he hath also rejected thee from being king."

Nah 3:4 — "Because of the multitude of the whoredoms of the wellfavoured harlot, the mistress of witchcrafts, that selleth nations through her whoredoms, and families through her witchcrafts."

Modern Corruption

The reigning modern claim — that there are “good witches” and that Wicca is a harmless, nature-loving religion — is a flat contradiction of Scripture, which knows no benign witchcraft.

expand to see more

Here the corruption is not drift but open defiance, and it must be met head-on. The modern witchcraft revival — Wicca, “green” and “kitchen” witchery, and the vast “witchtok” following that markets spell-kits to teenage girls — insists that a witch may be good, that her craft is mere earth-honoring ritual and self-empowerment, and that the Bible’s hostility is superstition or male oppression. Scripture grants none of it. It never distinguishes a white witch from a black; it forbids the art itself, root and branch, because every witch by definition seeks power the LORD has reserved to Himself and traffics, wittingly or not, with the powers of darkness. To bless what God curses is not compassion but rebellion.

The Word’s verdict is fixed, and its remedy is glorious. Witchcraft is ranked flatly among the works of the flesh — “idolatry, witchcraft” (Gal 5:20) — that bar men from the kingdom of God, and the unrepentant sorcerer is left outside the city (Rev 21:8). Yet the same Bible that says “thou shalt not suffer a witch to live” also records witches who lived — because they turned. At Ephesus former practitioners “brought their books together, and burned them before all men” (Act 19:19), and the word of God grew and prevailed. The gospel does not soften the sentence on witchcraft; it offers the witch a Saviour who bore that sentence, so that she may burn her craft not under judgment but in repentance and joy.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word is Old English wicce, a worker of sorcery — the root that modern “Wicca” revives.

expand to see more

Witch — from Old English wicce (feminine) and wicca (masculine).

It names a practitioner of sorcery, never a benign one in Scripture.

The law commands, “Thou shalt not suffer a witch to live” (Exo 22:18).

Samuel calls rebellion the sin of witchcraft (1Sa 15:23).

Nineveh, the mistress of witchcrafts, was razed for her sorceries (Nah 3:4).

Usage

"The AV witch is a real worker of sorcery under sentence of death, not a storybook hag or a harmless neighbor."

"Samuel weighs all rebellion by it: “rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft” (1Sa 15:23)."

"Modern “Wicca” revives the very word wicce — but Scripture allows no good witch."
